title: Hybrid Evidence Synthesis Combining Umbrella Review Principles with Narrative Synthesis of Recent High-Quality Original rs-fMRI Studies in mTBI
content: Background: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is frequently followed by persistent cognitive, af-fective, and sensory complaints despite unremarkable conventional structural imaging. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has been increasingly employed to detect subtle alterations in large-scale brain networks. However, variability in analytical approaches and the potential influence of neurovascular factors complicate interpretation of BOLD-derived connectivity findings. Objective: This review integrates umbrella-level evidence from systematic reviews and me-ta-analyses with a focused narrative synthesis of recent high-quality rs-fMRI studies in mTBI and repetitive head impact (RHI). The aim was to identify convergent patterns of network dysfunction while critically examining methodological constraints, including the absence of perfusion control and limited integration with task-based paradigms. Findings: Across evidence tiers, the most consistently implicated regions include core nodes of the default mode network (precuneus and posterior cingulate cortex), the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, insula, and cerebellum. Reported altera-tions—predominantly hypoconnectivity—have been associated with deficits in atten-tion, memory, executive function, fatigue, and affective regulation characteristic of post-concussion syndrome (PCS). Emerging data suggest partial convergence between resting-state and task-evoked dysfunction within these same circuits. Conclusion: Current evidence supports a network-level model of mTBI in which distributed con-nectivity disturbances contribute to persistent symptomatology. While rs-fMRI demonstrates sensitivity to subtle dysfunction, methodological heterogeneity and po-tential neurovascular confounds limit immediate clinical application. Future longitu-dinal and multimodal studies incorporating perfusion-sensitive techniques and task-based paradigms are required to clarify the neuronal specificity and translational value of these findings.
